content:
It’s been a long time since I posted on LinkedIn.
For months I poured everything into securing a seat in the LL.M. programe in International Climate Change and Environmental Law at Jigme Singye Wangchuck School of Law, Bhutan.
On the morning of 12 June 2026, I woke up with an email that changed everything. I had been selected with a fully funded scholarship from the Govt. of India. It remains the biggest academic achievement of my life so far. The excitement and motivation that filled me that day are still vivid.
All credit goes to my old friend Arshdeep Singh Gill, who guided me throughout the process and constantly offered fresh perspectives. I am genuinely grateful to you.
From a young age, the religious teachings of my late grandfather instilled in me a deep respect for the sacred bond between a man and nature. During my Bachelor of Laws, I had the opportunity to present findings on the 186th Report of the Law Commission of India, which recommended specialised courts for environmental matters. My research also highlighted India’s ranking of 176th out of 180 countries in the 2024 Environmental Performance Index.
What truly sparked my interest was learning that Bhutan is the only carbon-negative country in the world. A comparative study of the two constitutions deepened that curiosity. Article 5 of the Constitution of Bhutan is dedicated to the environment. It makes it a fundamental duty of every citizen to protect the natural environment and conserve biodiversity, while placing a clear obligation on the government to maintain a minimum of sixty per cent forest cover. In contrast, the Indian Constitution addresses environmental protection mainly through Article 48A and Article 51A(g) both non-justiciable. Over time, the Supreme Court of India has understood the importance of environment under Article 21.
The programme at JSW Law is built on an international framework, taught by professors from across the world. It promises meaningful cultural exchange, work with local communities, learning both inside and outside the classroom. Using Bhutan as a living case study of determined environmental conservation felt perfectly aligned with the specialised training I sought.
But the twist came afterwards, everything was set. I managed the financial challenges. Then, ten days before the flight, I fell ill. The doctor strictly advised against travel. Despite every effort, I had no choice but to inform the school. The disappointment that followed is difficult to put into words.
I remain deeply thankful to Jigme Singye Wangchuck School of Law for selecting me, and especially to Tandin Wangchuk sir and Tashi Tamo ma’am for their support. Their response once again showed that Bhutan is a truly citizen-centric nation, one that places the happiness and well-being of people at the centre.
This chapter did not unfold the way I had hoped. Yet the experience has only strengthened my resolve to keep contributing to meaningful climate action.
comment: Environmental law’s biggest challenge is often bridging constitutional commitments with enforcement on the ground. Comparative models like Bhutan can offer valuable lessons in institutional design and accountability.
